scenes.title: Which Blender did the code reach?

cues.text: A Blender tool call begins outside Blender, so its route is part of the explanation.
In this project, code reached Blender through a live connection, a background helper, or a direct command.
Each route could read a different scene state, even when the Python operation looked similar.
We will follow the request, identify its inputs, and separate the returned message from the evidence it contains.
Start with three layers: the Blender application, the supplied MCP bridge, and the project scripts.
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, exposes named tools to the client making the request.
The project launcher locates the add-on code and starts its local server on port nine eight seven six.
The project smoke test initializes a client session, lists the available tools, and submits a small scene query.
The bridge supplies communication; each project script defines the operation to perform.
The historical import used Blender four point five; the later MCP setup used Blender five point two point three.
An early background request failed because its process could not find an executable named Blender.
The helper first reads the Blender path override and otherwise falls back to that executable name.
Setting the override to the installed application path allowed later summary tools to return file information.
That retry supports a specific executable-lookup repair. A separate child-process workaround did not establish the same repair everywhere.
On the live route, the execution tool calls the connection helper with the submitted Python code.
The helper packages the code and serialization setting into a JSON request, followed by a message delimiter.
It sends that request through the local socket to the Blender add-on.
The response travels back with a status and either a result or an error message.
The code reads the scene available in that connected Blender process. Its identity and state matter to the result.

scenes.title: A smoke test has a narrow job

cues.text: The smoke test asks for the open file path and counts the objects whose type is mesh.
One recorded call completed at the tool level while its returned payload contained an error.
A later call returned the saved model path and twenty-four thousand, three hundred and fifty mesh objects.
These records establish communication and a scene inventory at those moments.
They do not check every surface or dimension. Object counts and unique mesh data-block counts also describe different things.
A direct command starts a separate Blender process and selects a saved file as its input.
The background option runs without the normal interface. A Python option then executes a script file or an expression.
The MCP background helper uses the expression route to run its result-handling wrapper.
Argument order matters: loading a file can replace settings applied earlier in the command.
The executable, file, script, logs and process exit code together identify this run.

scenes.title: Choose the file that represents the state

cues.text: Before the background helper launches Blender, it checks whether a connected instance has unsaved changes to the same file.
It compares normalized paths and reads the dirty-state flag from the live instance.
A matching dirty file takes a special branch: save a numbered temporary copy, then open that copy in the new process.
A clean file or a different open file leaves the supplied disk path as the input.
If the connection helper raises a connection error, this implementation also falls back to the supplied file on disk.
The temporary-copy branch uses the save operator with the copy option enabled.
It yields that new path to the background execution and attempts to remove the copy when the context exits.
A returned error status from the live query or save step raises an error instead of quietly selecting a successful result.
For review, record which branch was taken and which file the process actually opened.
The CLI wrapper expects the executed code to assign a dictionary to a variable called result.
It serializes that dictionary and prints a recognizable result marker into standard output.
The caller scans for a result marker or an error marker and reconstructs the response.
A historical diagnostic assigned a list instead. The recorded correction wrapped that list under a bounds key.
The retry returned structured bounds. This repaired the response format; the geometric meaning still depended on the diagnostic itself.
Keep four outcomes visible: request delivery, process completion, the script payload, and validation coverage.
A connection failure can prevent the submitted code from running at all.
A completed tool call can still contain an application error, as the early smoke test showed.
A returned pass field describes what the script claims; it does not reveal whether every required check ran.
The next examples show why combining these outcomes into one green badge would lose essential information.

scenes.title: A success marker can contradict the process

cues.text: The later audit found that the inspected helper accepts a result marker without first requiring a successful process return code.
The isolated test supplied a simulated completed process with return code one hundred and thirty-nine and a payload claiming a pass.
The unchanged helper returned that dictionary. The animation shows the same contradiction in its two inputs.
No Blender process was deliberately crashed for this test. It reproduced a result-handling gap using a mocked process result.
The correction plan therefore requires process status and payload status to be checked separately.
A separate project helper already uses a stronger execution gate when it supervises the vent checks.
It runs each step, reads the evidence file, and requires both a zero return code and a true passed field.
It records progress and stops the sequence when that condition fails.
That provides a useful code comparison. It does not mean the MCP wrapper was patched.
The planned wrapper correction also needs valid markers, useful logs and explicit handling of contradictory responses.
Even a completed verifier needs a coverage check.
The audit ran the screen-check loop with an empty screen register and a valid port root.
No screens were tested, yet the loop produced six pose rows that each claimed eight screens.
The proposed correction validates required identities and counts actual successful checks before reporting a pass.
This example concerns an isolated loop. It does not establish that the delivered model has missing screens.

scenes.title: A deadline is a separate kind of evidence

cues.text: Long operations introduced another boundary: the calling tool could reach its deadline before a useful result returned.
The historical trace records several roughly two-minute timeouts, followed by inspections and narrower or direct background retries.
A transport timeout alone does not establish the final process state or the validity of its output file.
Inspect the job and artifact evidence before deciding what to retry.
Likewise, a successful background workaround does not prove that the repeatedly disconnected live connection was permanently repaired.

scenes.title: A resource check needs the right context

cues.text: Summary tools have contracts too. Consider a checker that reports missing external files.
The inspected code resolves paths without passing the linked data-block’s library context.
In an audit fixture, a texture beside its linked library was reported missing beside the main file.
A separate tiled-image fixture also exposed an unreported missing secondary tile.
The planned correction resolves paths in their owning library and enumerates the resources that are actually required.
Many supporting tools ran outside Blender: numerical fitting, image preparation, CAD conversion and report packaging.
Their outputs became files or manifests consumed by a later Blender operation.
The vent supervisor makes this split concrete: its contour step uses the host Python interpreter, while other steps launch Blender.
Inside Blender, scripts can inspect or change scene data through its Python API.
Recording the producer, input file and consumer keeps these dependencies visible across process boundaries.
The historical plan split official references, supplementary references and scene auditing into parallel assignments.
A coordinator used their evidence to guide an editor working on the model.
The early audit produced multiple views, including this archived three-quarter render and top view.
Those views supported inspection of the visible geometry; controlled lighting was later added for materials and small surface details.
Parallel research expands the evidence, while coordinated editing keeps the intended model state understandable.
For each operation, carry forward its runtime, file or scene, inputs, read or write scope, outputs and validation coverage.
Keep the exact attempt and its result attached to the script that produced it.
The history tells us what happened; the current source explains the inspected implementation; the audit identifies remaining gaps.
With those distinctions in place, we can now examine the model hierarchy and understand what the geometry tools actually changed.
